caption:
You buy a 1TB laptop. It shows 931GB. Did they scam you? 👀

Nope, there's a reason 👇

💾 Drive makers count in decimal: 1 TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes
🖥️ Windows counts in binary: 1 "GB" = 1,073,741,824 bytes (2³⁰)
➗ 1 trillion ÷ 1024 ÷ 1024 ÷ 1024 = 931.3, which Windows still labels "GB"

The gap grows with size: ~2% at KB, ~7% at GB, ~10% at TB.

⚖️ It went to court: Western Digital settled in 2006, Seagate offered refunds in 2007.
📖 The binary unit has a proper name, the "gibibyte" (GiB). Almost nobody uses it.
🍎 macOS has counted in decimal since 2009, so the same drive shows 1 TB on a Mac.

Follow for more on why things are the way they are.

scenes.say: You finally buy a 1 terabyte laptop. You open your files, and it says 931 gigabytes. Wait. Did they scam you?
Nope. There's actually a reason for that.
Your drive and your computer are counting in two different languages.
Computers think in powers of two. 2 to the power of 10 is 1,024{ten twenty four}, so early engineers called that a kilobyte. Close enough to a thousand, right?
But the gap grows. 2% at kilobytes, 7% at gigabytes, almost 10% at terabytes.
Drive makers use the metric meaning. 1 terabyte is a trillion bytes. Windows divides by 1,024{ten twenty four}, three times, gets 931, and still calls it gigabytes.
It confused so many people, it went to court. Western Digital settled in 2006{two thousand six}, and Seagate offered refunds in 2007{two thousand seven}.
There's even a proper name for the binary version: the gibibyte. Almost nobody uses it. And since 2009{two thousand nine}, Macs count in decimal, so the same drive shows 1 terabyte on a Mac.
Same drive. Same bytes. Just a different way of counting. Follow, and I'll tell you why things are the way they are.
